nameStory: The name 'prickly fanpetals' perfectly captures this plant's key features - the small spines or 'prickles' that dot its stems, and the fan-shaped arrangement of its narrow petals. The scientific name 'Sida spinosa' reinforces this, with 'spinosa' meaning spiny or thorny in Latin.
description: Prickly fanpetals is a small, weedy plant that grows as either an annual herb or short-lived shrub, reaching 8 inches to about 3 feet tall. It has a bushy, spreading growth habit with multiple stems branching from the base. The plant produces small yellow-orange flowers and has distinctive small spines along its stems, giving it a somewhat rough appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow to pale orange flowers about half an inch across with five narrow petals arranged in a fan shape. The petals feel papery and delicate to the touch, and flowers appear singly or in small clusters along the stems.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Alternate leaves are oval to lance-shaped with toothed edges, feeling somewhat rough and fuzzy when rubbed between your fingers. They're typically 1-3 inches long with prominent veining.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a low, bushy plant with multiple branching stems that spread outward from the base, giving it a somewhat sprawling appearance in disturbed soils.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems feel rough to the touch due to small, sharp spines scattered along their length - run your finger carefully along a stem and you'll feel these tiny prickles catch slightly.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, segmented seed pods that split apart when ripe, each segment containing one seed. The pods feel dry and papery when mature.

habitat: In New England, prickly fanpetals is extremely rare, found only in highly disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, and waste ground where the soil has been compacted or disturbed. It prefers full sun and tolerates poor, dry soils. Given its tropical origins, it's likely only found in the warmer, southern parts of New England during exceptional years.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil temperatures warm up, producing small rosettes of fuzzy leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Active growing season with stems elongating and small yellow flowers appearing continuously from mid-summer onward in warm weather.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering until first frost, producing seed pods that mature and split open to release seeds for next year's growth.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to potentially germinate the following spring if conditions are right.

funFact: This little plant is one of the most widely traveled species on Earth - it's native to tropical regions on multiple continents and has hitchhiked its way around the globe, yet it's so rare in New England that it's been spotted only once in our region!
confusionNotes: The small yellow flowers might be confused with other weedy mallows, but the distinctive small spines on the stems are the dead giveaway - carefully run your finger along the stem and you'll feel the prickles that give this plant its name.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the Mallow family (same as hollyhocks and hibiscus), prickly fanpetals looks nothing like its showy garden relatives. This highlights how diverse plant families can be - from tiny weedy annuals to large tropical flowering shrubs.
compareHints: Since this is the only Sida species recorded in New England, compare it to other small mallows in the region. Unlike common mallow which has deeply lobed leaves and larger pink flowers, prickly fanpetals has unlobed toothed leaves, smaller yellow flowers, and those diagnostic stem spines that other regional mallows lack.
